Clytemnestra. The queen of Argos who murdered her husband Agamemnon upon his return from the Trojan War, one of mythology's most complex and powerful figures.

Clytemnestra was queen of Argos and sister to Helen, sharing royal blood and watching her sister become the cause of a ten-year war. Her first marriage was to Tantalus, a man whom Agamemnon slew before taking her as his own wife, so her marriage began in violence and grief. For a decade while Agamemnon commanded the Greek forces at Troy, Clytemnestra ruled Argos alone, bearing the burden of kingship on her shoulders.

During his long absence, she took a lover named Aegisthus, finding solace and alliance in his arms. When Agamemnon returned triumphantly from Troy, Clytemnestra murdered him. Whether she acted to avenge his willingness to sacrifice their daughter Iphigenia or from passion and political ambition, the deed changed everything. She also killed Cassandra, the Trojan princess Agamemnon had brought home as a war prize, in a fury of jealousy and betrayal. With Aegisthus at her side, Clytemnestra ruled for years until her children grew old enough to avenge their father's death.

She was bound to Agamemnon, the husband whose death she orchestrated, and to Helen of Troy, her sister whose beauty set the war in motion and left her kingdom vulnerable. Cassandra, the woman she murdered, was a war prize and symbol of her husband's infidelity. The Trojan War itself was the conflict that separated her from Agamemnon and transformed her into his nemesis.
